Teen Genius- Brandon Kynoch

By: Sophia Phirippides | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A genius in the tech world is a rarerity and as good as gold. At just 16 years of age Brandon Kynoch looks set to change the world as a gaming developer

Unique Selling Point:
Every once in a while a genius comes along and changes the world. From Bill Gates, Steve Jobs to Elon Musk they all affected the evolving world through their innovations. Brandon Kynoch is one such kid, at the age of sixteen he has over a hundred thousand people across the world tapping their fingers to his imagination, a feat most us can only dream of in a lifetime.



Summary:
Within 24 hours of its launch, Torus, a digital game had already achieved one hundred thousand downloads on the Apple ITunes across at least 134 countries in the world, a huge achievement in the gaming world especially coming from a teenager. The game has taken off by storm making everyone in the software development industry take notice and believe that at just the tender age of 16 years, Brandon’s possibilities are endless. Apple apps listed the game as app of the day on their AppStore.

Brandon is a 16-year-old St Stithians schoolboy from Johannesburg who is a 100% self-taught in coding and game development. Torus is the second game he has developed. At the age of 13 he did all the online courses on the internet and when there was nothing more on the internet to teach him coding and game development he went to a IT professor at Wits who gave him very advanced books to study. Dr. Richard Klein was immensely impressed by Brandon’s work and dedication.


Further information:
Brandon’s creative interest began at the age of seven where he was already a painter. He gradually developed an appetite for digital art and graphic design and by the age of 11 he was doing 3D art and photorealistic renderings that helped enhance his skills.
When Brandon turned 13 he shifted his focus to programming where he began developing apps and small games for fun. ‘Blast: A Tank Game’ was the first game that Brandon had ever published. It started out as just another small game that he was developing for fun, but soon realized that it had a lot of potential. The game had 6000 downloads in it’s first 24hours. Brandon has since opened his own game design studio, which his latest game Torus was developed under.
At 16 years of age now, the wiz kid has already participated at international Expos, featured twice on an internationally distributed 3D Artist Magazine and is a huge inspiration to his peers in the country. He has shown that anything is possible if you dream and work hard at it. With aspirations of owning his own gaming studio, the sky is definitely the limit for the kid and he is on track, but how did he do it? Carte Blanche finds out…

Press Release:


Sixteen year old software wiz kid, Brandon Kynoch is a self taught phenom. His second mobile game 'Torus' shot up to a hundred thousand downloads on the Apple App Store within 24 hours. Competing against about 50 million games this is quite a feat, especially for someone so young, working as a sole developer. Developing a mobile game needs a strategic mind equipped with computer coding knowledge, design flair and business acumen. Brandon has it all.

Script:


Intro shots of Torus being played, screenshots, kids playing… 10 seconds

VO: Torus is a new mobile puzzle game where you connect the dots,while avoiding danger, testing your reaction speed and reflexes and it’s taking the gaming world by storm.// 16 year old St Stithian’s pupil, Brandon Kynoch is it’s creator.

Brandon: Growing up I have always been interested in video games and I love playing them, one day I decided I am going to make my own.

Vox Pop: Kid… about how addictive the game is… no transcripts

kids vox pops - something about Brandon’s game being addictive

Costa: It’s a very clever way he has done things because the more you play and the better you get the more you almost end up encouraging yourself to do better and the way he has been able to grab onto that and bring that out in the game is genius

VO: Costa Tzingakis CEO of Red Oxygen, a mobile game development studio in Johannesburg, assessed Brandon’s game independently.

Costa: I think Torus is a good example of a very stimulating game, it is actually one of those that challenge your mind, its mental gymnastics.
Its perceived simplicity is one of its major assets which makes it so successful, less is more and really that makes the game

Link: It was named Apple’s App store game of the day in 137 countries worldwide and with over 100 000 downloads within 24 hours of launching, Brandon's second game Torus seems to have the world tapping their fingers.

Vox pop…. the kids saying why they love the game…

Costa: There is something like 50m plus games that he is competing against so yo be able to be app of the day and to be pushed right to the top of a very big pile that takes quite a thing.

Brandon: I had stayed up until midnight waiting to see the App store refresh and I went on and there it was as game of the day.

Mac: How big is gaming n the country and globally

Costa: Gaming is the fourth biggest entertainment industry in the world it did about 108 b dollars last year, it is about to become the third biggest overtaking tv. In SA its overtaken music movies and tv.

VO: So Brandon is competing in the premier league of entertainment, and his mother Nicky has been cheering his highpoints from the side-lines.

Nicky: One of them was sitting next to him when torus launched and having the joy of seeing the game go live and you just see the screens go live.

VO: Brandon started teaching himself computer coding at the age of 11, with the support and encouragement of his somewhat bemused parents.

Nicky: He was downloading 1500 page manuals and sourcing through that and using what findings he needed to advance, so that’s quite remarkable.

Alan: To just watch him put that code in and look at those lines I know nothing about it and its bracket A and a plus, I enjoy watching it.

VO: But it was Brandon’s creative side that first piqued his teachers’ interest when he was just seven years old.

Nicky: The school phoned us one day and said he is artistically gifted please come along and have a look, and it just evolved from there.

Brandon: I think the first real project that I had worked on start to finish was a photo realistic render, I had actually sent that off to a magazine based in London, called 3D artist and they published it in that magazine.

VO: Brandon was then inspired to combine his artistic talents and his love of computing into creating his own mobile games.

Brandon: I learnt everything off of free learning services on the internet. I think that’s really the best way to learn, through experimenting.

VO: At fourteen he started creating his first game, Blast, combining his artistic and coding skills. But being self taught, he hit a hitch when it came to certain algorithmic programming he needed for the game.

Nicky: At some stage towards the the end of grade seven, he said mom I am running out of learning resources, and then I found doctor Richard Klein from computer science and applied maths from Wits.

Richard: I had this one interaction with him where we sat down and discussed I helped point him in the right direction give him the resources and really from there he has done everything himself.

Mac: What books did he give you that was helpful

Brandon: These two computer science books which I ordered online and they are just a great reference for when I get stuck. This one is a bible for all algorithms.

VO: Brandon then rewrote a complicated cooperative path finding algorithm, so that Blast could allow for agents of different sizes traveling at different speeds.

Brandon: So cooperative path finding is the kind of thing you see in advanced computer simulations and obviously video games.

Richard: This is the first time i have seen someone that age teaching themselves the algorithms and the maths that really are far beyond what you would do at school.

Brandon: I took all the code from my game and written up documentation on it and entered that into the eskom science expo which took me all the way to nationals and I also won two scholarships and a cash prize.

VO: It took Brandon two years to develop Blast, with coding and doing all the graphics himself. It only received 6000 downloads, but it had attracted Apple’s attention. One day in class Brandon received an email from them, saying they would like to get updates from him.

Brandon: Its actually funny, the whole time people get this image that I am like a professional studio with hundreds of employees, that was one of their questions, was how many employees do you have?

VO: But Brandon’s next game Torus, only took three weeks of development, which was a game changer.

Brandon: I think it’s also amazing to see something that I worked on for 2 years, wasn't necessarily that successful and then a game like torus which was just 3 weeks could do so well.

Link: Experts believe that it is uncommon for a game of this quality to be fully developed by just one person, most game developing businesses work in large teams.

Costa: You need to bare in mind many game companies mobile game companies have 800 plus employees, and you have got one young boy making something on his own.

VO: The psychology behind creating a successful mobile game can be elusive, it isn’t a hard and fast science.

Costa: We ourselves do a lot of research into the psych of gaming and it depends a lot on the type of game you are making, and if you dont understand the way people think to make a game that appeals and is successful is quite difficult.

Brandon: After releasing blast I realized players loved the game but that enjoyment would die out very quickly I had done a lot of research into game design and what makes people enjoy games and I am not going to share the secrets but I added a lot of those things into Torus.

Costa: One of the things that really jumps out at me is as you move through the game you join the dots quicker the music and the sound matches to that and creates a lovely symphony those kind of small things that you don't necessarily think of all meshed together to make a fantastic experience.

Mac: What’s next

Brandon: Right now I just want to keep focusing on developing these small games like torus I do still have school unfortunately I really want to build my own studio to the point I have full time employees and I can release games often and that’s my dream.

Nicky: He is a good example of a child who has not followed his dreams he has chased after them.
